items.summary: Historical maps contain dense morphological and semantic information about past urban environments, but many digitization workflows focus primarily on extracting geometry, and do not capture cartographic semantics such as building use and construction materials. This study introduces ArchiveLens, a generative spatial knowledge framework that operationalizes historical maps as entity-centric, machine-queryable geospatial databases. The pipeline decouples morphological and semantic reconstruction through three stages: tiled YOLOv11-seg instance segmentation for building footprint extraction; deterministic material classification via hue, saturation, and value (HSV)-based color thresholds; and localized attribute parsing using a quantized vision-language model constrained by domain-specific prompts. Extracted entities are integrated into a hybrid Spatial-Temporal Retrieval-Augmented Generation (ST-RAG) architecture that combines dense semantic retrieval with symbolic spatio-temporal filtering and mandatory provenance grounding. Applied to 445 georeferenced Sanborn map sheets of Chicago (1918-1950), the framework achieves high geometric and semantic accuracy. Beyond performance, ArchiveLens advances GIScience by formalizing historical cartography as structured spatial knowledge representation, allowing researchers to query building attributes and compare spatial patterns across map sheets and years.
items.title: ArchiveLens: A Generative Spatial Knowledge Framework for Semantic Reconstruction of Historical Maps

items.summary: Deepwave provides wave propagation modules for PyTorch, for applications such as seismic imaging and inversion. It performs forward modelling and backpropagation, so it can simulate wave propagation to generate synthetic data, or invert for the scattering potential (reverse-time migration, RTM, or its least-squares counterpart, LSRTM), other model parameters (full-waveform inversion, FWI), initial wavefields, or source wavelets. It can also be used inside a larger chain of operations, with forward and backpropagation flowing through the whole chain end to end. You can use your own objective functions, or functions that generate the propagator's inputs, and PyTorch's automatic differentiation calculates how to backpropagate through them. New to seismic/wave-equation terminology? The glossary defines the terms (PML, CFL, Born, FWI, and more) used throughout this README and the rest of the documentation. Deepwave requires Python 3.9 or later and PyTorch 2.4 or later. First install PyTorch for your CPU or CUDA device using the instructions on the PyTorch website . Then install Deepwave: pip install deepwave   macOS wheels support Apple Silicon. Intel Mac wheels are no longer provided: PyTorch 2.4 and newer do not publish wheels for that platform. Prebuilt x86 wheels require AVX2. Older CPUs need a source build; see installation troubleshooting . PyTorch is Deepwave's only dependency. The example scripts under docs/ additionally import matplotlib (to draw their figures) and, in some cases, numpy , scipy (smoothing and filter design), torchaudio (applying those filters), torchvision and geomloss , but those are needed only to run the examples, never by Deepwave itself. To install all of them: pip install 'deepwave[examples]'   The documentation contains examples and instructions on how to install and use Deepwave. You might also like to watch a video summary of Deepwave . Not every propagator supports every option (dimensionality, backend, boundary faces, batching, second-order differentiation, callbacks, ...). See the capability matrix (declared in the code and checked by conformance tests) before assuming a combination works. Why Deepwave Computationally efficient. Deepwave's compiled kernels use a hand-derived adjoint for better performance and lower memory requirements than pure PyTorch implementations. See what Deepwave calculates . Second derivatives are supported, not just first. The scalar, acoustic, and elastic propagators can compute Hessian-vector products (derivatives of gradients); see the Hessian example . Born (linearised) modelling. Model scattered waves from perturbations to a background medium for linearised inversion and imaging. See the torch.func example . Deepwave fits into an ordinary PyTorch workflow. Because propagation is a normal PyTorch autograd Function , it works directly with PyTorch optimisers, DistributedDataParallel over shots, torch.func transforms, and any PyTorch loss function or neural-network model of the input parameters. See the capability matrix for exactly what each propagator supports. Deepwave does not try to be a general symbolic PDE solver, a multi-node HPC code, or a non-differentiable simulation toolkit — see Devito , SPECFEM , and k-Wave respectively for those needs. If you are choosing between wave-propagation packages, see the comparison guide . (Note: the DeepWave-KAUST GitHub organisation, home of the SWEEP package, is unrelated to this project.) Features Supports the 1D, 2D, and 3D constant density acoustic / scalar wave equation (regular and Born modelling), variable density acoustic, elastic, viscoacoustic (single-mechanism SLS attenuation), elastic VTI (anisotropic), and pseudo-acoustic VTI ( deepwave.acoustic_vti , the Duveneck et al. 2008 V_S=0 reduction) wave equations Runs on CPUs and appropriate GPUs The gradient of all outputs (final wavefields and receiver data) can be calculated with respect to the model parameters (wavespeed, scattering potential, etc

items.summary: EXTERNAL QIGONG AND HUMAN THERMAL RADIATION PATTERNS AT THE LIMIT is a 777-page English research working monograph investigating whether thermographic differences observed during culturally defined qigong and matched neutral tasks can be distinguished from ordinary human thermoregulation, environmental exchange and measurement bias. The governing three-coupling is infrared thermal imaging x physiological regulation x heat-transfer models. The research treats “external qi” as a cultural and experimental task label, not an established physical energy carrier. The scientific core separates raw infrared radiance from inferred skin temperature and estimated heat flux. It develops emissivity and reflected-wall correction, blackbody calibration, spectral detector response, conduction and perfusion bioheat models, convection, evaporation, respiration-related temperature patterns, posture and muscular activity. The original candidate bulk heat equation is explicitly refined by separating volumetric tissue transport from surface heat-transfer boundary conditions. The principal proposed test uses concealed task assignments, matched breathing/movement/clothing, phantom references, negative-control regions and conventional physics-first rivals. Thirty physically distinct mathematical plates document governing relationships, units, assumptions, identifiability, masked falsifiers and chapter links. Eighty-two independent research chapters contain 410 single-page investigations. The true center of the monograph is its 200 one-page Research Gates, each posing a falsifiable question in bold deep-navy typography and asking what an independent successor must measure, challenge, disprove or preserve. Thirty-three differentiated Phoenix Answer Embryos propose future instruments, error-correction artifacts, negative-result protocols and reproducibility tools. The DOI registry separates three STARLI author mother volumes from eleven externally published methodological or conventional-science references on infrared thermography, emissivity, classical bioheat and research design. Bibliographic sources constrain methods; they do not validate extraordinary qigong mechanisms. Every integrated experiment is prospective. The book presents no completed human intervention, clinically established effect, new physical particle or evidence of treatment efficacy. Ethical authorization and independent scientific review would be required before future human-observation research. items.summary: Multivariate time series produced by industrial installations and server clusters are under continuous monitoring, and anomaly detection is the first line of defense before a local fault escalates into a system-wide failure. In the absence of labels, the dominant paradigm trains a reconstruction model on normal data and scores the residual to reach a verdict. Recent work has steadily enriched the expressiveness of the recovery map through Transformers, diffusion models, and cross-scale associations. A residual, however, only certifies that an observation can be recovered; it does not certify that the variables still explain one another as they do under normal operation. A coordinated yet unfamiliar operating transition inflates the residual without breaking any relationship, whereas a sensor drifting away from its peers may leave the residual silent. Methods that fold inter-variable dependencies into the reconstruction objective inherit this ambiguity, because their relational evidence is ultimately supervised by the same recovery loss. We therefore propose CLOSURE, which evaluates recoverability and cross-channel consistency as two normal-data prediction tasks learned in separation. The recoverability task is solved by a diffusion reconstructor conditioned on a discrete memory of normal temporal bases. The consistency task is solved by a relation-closure operator that predicts every channel exclusively from the others, where the target's own trajectory is withheld and sparse signed gates decide which peers are actually used. The two scores are reconciled only through calibration on normal data. Extensive experiments show that CLOSURE consistently outperforms recent reconstruction-, frequency-, and topology-based detectors on public benchmark streams, confirming the value of examining consistency alongside recoverability.
items.title: CLOSURE: Cross-Channel Closure for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection

items.summary: On million-node graphs, the memory wall arrives before the compute wall: a GNN that never fits in VRAM cannot deliver the all-node inference its accuracy promises. The standard remedy, pruning, has always been an accuracy tax - paid once and never refunded. DPR refuses this framing. Its central insight is that the mask that shrinks training can also scaffold recovery: one compact node set bounds both computations of graph learning, serving as the encoder's training graph and, at inference, as the anchor from which a sparse structure-aware decoder rebuilds every pruned node (double-layer sparsification). The order is inverted - prune for efficiency, then reconstruct for accuracy - and the tax is repaid: the deployed 30%-budget model trains in 1,450 MiB of peak memory on one 6 GB GPU and recovers 96.9% of its dense-reconstruction reference, beating a same-GPU rerun of the edge-sparsification baseline DSpar by +1.36 pp at 50.1% lower peak training memory; against the same-protocol full-batch no-prune encoder the deployed point pays a measured 2.64 pp accuracy tax for a 2.8x smaller training footprint. Pruning without reconstruction leaves the encoder at 0.378 within the same 40-epoch window (Fig. 4), and all-node serving runs 46x faster than sampling-based GraphSAGE, giving up approx. 5.4 pp of test accuracy. The framework scales to a 2.45M-node production graph at 6,285 MiB of peak training memory; extended variants (long-range context, external text features, a CAN-bus application) are reported as extensions and do not compete with the deployed method, and the 41.8%-budget M4 point, scored on a coarsened super-node graph with its own split, is reported separately rather than compared with the original-node baselines. DPR thus turns aggressive node pruning from an accuracy tax into a safe training accelerator for VRAM-limited all-node inference.
items.title: Decoupled Prune-and-Reconstruct: Training on a Compact Core with Double-Layer Sparsification

items.summary: SimilCode Benchmark is a curated dataset of 120 short source-code snippets in C# and Java, organised into 60 test-case pairs per language across four ground-truth similarity categories (identical, functional, structural, and different) with fifteen reference groups per language. Every pair was independently classified by two raters blind to the original labels, with near-perfect inter-rater agreement (Cohen's κ = 0.989). All code was authored specifically for this study or drawn from the public domain; no student-submitted code is included. The dataset was used to benchmark four contemporary commercial large language models as similarity analysts — claude-opus-5 , gpt-5.5-2026-04-23 , gemini-3.1-pro-preview and deepseek-v4-pro — with three independent replicates per case–model combination, yielding 1,440 evaluations. The same 120 pairs were also processed with three established classical detectors drawn from three distinct algorithmic families: Moss (winnowing fingerprints), JPlag v6.3.0 (token-string matching) and Dolos v2.9.3 (tree-sitter syntax trees). The record further includes a separate corpus for validating algorithmic-complexity (Big O) estimation: 40 canonical algorithms and 8 adversarial cases designed to defeat surface cues such as misleading identifiers, unreachable code and memoisation. Raw model responses, classical-detector outputs, the standardised prompt with its SHA-256 checksum, the ground-truth tables and the analysis scripts are published together for reproducibility.
items.title: SimilCode Benchmark: A Dual-Language Source-Code Similarity Dataset for the Evaluation of AI-Based Detectors

items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly automate complex tasks, with multi-agent systems seeking further performance gains through specialization and collaboration. However, distributing work across agents does not automatically yield complementary contributions, and inter-agent dependencies can turn local errors into task failure. To address these challenges, we propose AutoSwarm, a multi-agent framework for collaborative problem solving. Collaboration formation jointly defines responsibility boundaries and conditions for acceptance and downstream use, grounding capability allocation in contributions that other agents can assess and integrate toward a shared objective. Execution coordination couples agents' local progress through a shared state, using dependencies and supervisory relationships to govern agent activation, result handoffs, and integration while adapting subsequent actions to review feedback and emerging blockers. Experiments spanning long-horizon programming, interactive planning, and professional financial analysis demonstrate AutoSwarm's advantages over single-agent baselines and existing multi-agent frameworks. Source code is available at https://github.com/HKUDS/AutoSwarm.
items.title: AutoSwarm: Automating Agent Swarms

items.summary: Memory enables language agents to carry useful distinctions from past experience into future decisions. Its value depends on which distinctions survive, whether a bounded agent can use them, and what can be recovered or revised as demands evolve. We develop a decision-theoretic framework that follows this value from raw history through persistent state, operational use, and costly recovery and revision. Original and retained value are expressed in units of avoided task loss; risk-cost frontiers describe attainable recovery and preservation across uses. Unknown demand yields value profiles, while interactive feedback changes the distribution of future work. A cost-aware simulation condition and five minimal counterexamples expose the roles of information timing, retrieval access, component interaction, feedback and demand uncertainty. In particular, a pointer with zero mutual information about the answer can still reduce the cost of exact recovery. Diagnostics on LoCoMo, a two-project update task and longitudinal cases exhibit failures of preservation, use and measurement. At fixed retrieved evidence, a saved ledger changes subsequent answers; at fixed agent outputs, an evaluator revision changes scores. The framework connects these distinctions to operational risk bounds and testable principles for allocating memory, preserving recovery options and revising evidence dependencies.
items.title: The Value of Memory in Language Agents

items.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) rely on role-specific prompts and execution models to solve complex tasks collaboratively. However, prompt optimization typically keeps model assignments fixed, leaving differences in role requirements and their associated inference costs outside the search. We present UniMASO, a Unified framework for heterogeneous Multi-Agent System Optimization through the joint adaptation of prompts and model assignments. UniMASO evaluates candidate updates through local, downstream, and global feedback, using cost-aware Pareto search to retain useful quality-cost trade-offs. Topology-aware co-evolution then coordinates these updates according to agent roles and dependencies. Cross-level trajectory memory further supplies historical successes and failures to guide subsequent optimization. Experiments on five benchmarks and five execution topologies show that UniMASO achieves competitive task performance at substantially lower deployment cost than the strongest homogeneous configurations. Under centralized execution, it improves the average score from 69.79 to 70.40 while reducing token-weighted deployment cost by 85.2% relative to DeepSeek-V4-Pro with MASPO. These results support joint prompt-model adaptation as an effective approach to efficient multi-agent collaboration. The code is available at https://github.com/Achilles008/UniMASO_main.
items.title: Not Every Agent Needs the Strongest Model: Unified Prompt-Model Optimization for Heterogeneous LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems

items.summary: Host-based intrusion detectors order events, window audit streams and sequence attack stages by their timestamps. Every conclusion they draw therefore rests on assumptions about clocks, delivery, entity identity and the integrity of the evidence, and most of these assumptions go unstated. This Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) makes them explicit. Drawing on temporal databases, stream processing and runtime verification, we distill five components of a time model, together with a checklist of evidence assumptions and four levels of guarantee, and walk through a running campaign with them. A documented search yields fifteen families of detection and investigation. For papers selected by screening role and period, plus named systems and landmarks, we check the stated assumptions in the full texts, and we assess eleven temporal knowledge representation and reasoning (KRR) formalisms and a learned baseline on nine attack patterns. Some early alert correlators stated clock and delivery assumptions, and forensics measures clock error. Current provenance-based detectors state no clock bound. Four audited papers describe input-ordering conditions or conventions, but none specifies conditions for conclusion validity across a stated class of delivery failures. In the selected provenance-based systems, campaign composition uses system-specific procedures or objectives, learned state, causal graph queries or language models, and beyond CEP-based query systems, we found no temporal rule language or stream reasoner from KRR applied to host audit data. In 28 of 38 audited provenance-era detector papers, capture or stored evidence is trusted or its manipulation is placed out of scope, and none says which conclusions survive deleted, delayed or forged records. items.summary: Test-Time Prompt Tuning (TPT) adapts large pretrained models to unseen target distribution shifts by updating only lightweight prompt tokens. Existing TPT methods are effective, but they mainly optimize each prompt update locally. Across test-time steps, prompts updated at the current step are reused for the corresponding predictions and updates, so noisy or biased unlabeled objectives can accumulate and destabilize the prompt-update trajectory. We identify two failure modes: magnitude expansion, where updates move the prompt too far, and directional drift, where consecutive updates point in inconsistent directions. To analyze and control these failures, we propose Test-Time Prompt-Agnostic Decomposition ($\mathtt{TPD}$), which characterizes observed prompt-update trajectories from a dynamical-systems view and decomposes base prompt updates into magnitude and direction. $\mathtt{TPD}$ computes a spectral radius to measure update expansion and decomposes update directions into persistent, oscillatory, and residual components. Building on this decomposition, Adaptive Koopman Control ($\mathtt{AKC}$) regulates update magnitude by shrinking updates under expansive recent dynamics, while Hankel Update Router ($\mathtt{HUR}$) refines update direction by preserving persistent components and suppressing oscillatory and residual components. Together, $\mathtt{AKC}$ and $\mathtt{HUR}$ produce a stabilized prompt update. As a prompt-agnostic framework, $\mathtt{TPD}$ can be plugged into visual and text TPT methods without modifying the backbone, prompt architecture, or adaptation loss. Experiments on 15 datasets show that $\mathtt{TPD}$ consistently improves 10 baselines, with accuracy gains of $3$--$8\%$ for visual prompts and over $2\%$ for text prompts.
items.title: Test-Time Prompt-Agnostic Decomposition

items.summary: Disease surveillance increasingly integrates automated data collection, yet predefined sources and procedures require manual adaptation as reporting practices change. We explore agentic artificial intelligence (AI) as an approach to coordinating surveillance data collection across heterogeneous sources. Specifically, we built a multi-agent framework that integrates source discovery, source assessment, evidence structuring, event linking, and validation. Three retrospective applications illustrate its promise. The workflow recovered all 13 individual cases in a hantavirus outbreak, with links to 85 distinct publisher domains compared with 28 in the reference benchmark, reconstructed Canadian measles counts with a final total 0.33% below the national reference and higher cumulative counts on 79.8% of comparable days, and increased the share of days with recent Sierra Leone mpox reports from 28.2% to 65.6% by incorporating attributed media. These demonstrations also reveal limitations in record completeness and accuracy, while prospective gains in timeliness remain untested. We envision agentic AI as a complementary layer of public health data infrastructure, coordinating evidence-linked collection under surveillance goals and standards defined by public health professionals.
items.title: Toward an Agentic AI Approach to Public Health Data Collection

items.summary: Edge-centric IoT systems are increasingly evaluated through sensor values or platform features, yet the telemetry pipeline itself, the sequence of sensing, serialization, message mediation, ingestion, and persistence, is rarely released as a measurable object. This limits reproducible benchmarking of timeliness, provenance, and operational cost, especially in early-stage IoT design where real deployments and high-quality open data are often unavailable. I present a measurement-first edge IoT testbed and dataset that elevate timeliness, provenance, and energy to first-class telemetry dimensions. The testbed operationalizes a role-based event-driven architecture with explicit Source-Broker-Aggregator responsibilities and a schema-governed TelemetryMessage envelope (Avro) that embeds correlation identifiers and a uniform, cross-role vocabulary of stage-level timestamps. To trace mediation effects, I extend an MQTT broker (Eclipse Mosquitto) with a plugin that annotates messages with high-precision ingress/egress timestamps. I release the dataset in a dual representation: (i) replayable raw events as compressed Avro streams and (ii) analysis-ready long-format Parquet tables partitioned for efficient query and benchmarking, generated by a deterministic raw-to-tabular transformation pipeline. The contribution is an integrated engineering artifact and dataset built from established components. The demonstration describes one deployment through latency summaries, measurement-context distributions, and energy aggregates; it does not establish a new attribution method or a controlled performance benchmark. By co-releasing heterogeneous telemetry with pipeline timing and energy signals in both replayable and queryable forms, the artifact provides a basis for reproducible exploratory analysis and subsequent benchmarking studies.
items.title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking

items.summary: EXTERNAL QIGONG AND HUMAN THERMAL RADIATION PATTERNS AT THE LIMIT is a 777-page English research working monograph investigating whether thermographic differences observed during culturally defined qigong and matched neutral tasks can be distinguished from ordinary human thermoregulation, environmental exchange and measurement bias. The governing three-coupling is infrared thermal imaging x physiological regulation x heat-transfer models. The research treats “external qi” as a cultural and experimental task label, not an established physical energy carrier. The scientific core separates raw infrared radiance from inferred skin temperature and estimated heat flux. It develops emissivity and reflected-wall correction, blackbody calibration, spectral detector response, conduction and perfusion bioheat models, convection, evaporation, respiration-related temperature patterns, posture and muscular activity. The original candidate bulk heat equation is explicitly refined by separating volumetric tissue transport from surface heat-transfer boundary conditions. The principal proposed test uses concealed task assignments, matched breathing/movement/clothing, phantom references, negative-control regions and conventional physics-first rivals. Thirty physically distinct mathematical plates document governing relationships, units, assumptions, identifiability, masked falsifiers and chapter links. Eighty-two independent research chapters contain 410 single-page investigations. The true center of the monograph is its 200 one-page Research Gates, each posing a falsifiable question in bold deep-navy typography and asking what an independent successor must measure, challenge, disprove or preserve. Thirty-three differentiated Phoenix Answer Embryos propose future instruments, error-correction artifacts, negative-result protocols and reproducibility tools. The DOI registry separates three STARLI author mother volumes from eleven externally published methodological or conventional-science references on infrared thermography, emissivity, classical bioheat and research design. Bibliographic sources constrain methods; they do not validate extraordinary qigong mechanisms. Every integrated experiment is prospective. The book presents no completed human intervention, clinically established effect, new physical particle or evidence of treatment efficacy. Ethical authorization and independent scientific review would be required before future human-observation research. items.summary: Autonomous agents are increasingly deployed across sequences of related tasks, yet they often fail to retain and improve their knowledge over time. Existing approaches convert interaction trajectories into memories or reusable skills, but experience is not automatically reliable knowledge. Automatically collected skills and memories can propagate errors, mislead, and corrupt useful knowledge. To address this gap, we introduce Knowledge Evolution from Expertise and Lessons (KEEL), an agent-agnostic framework that uses verifier evidence to transform successful behavior into reusable skills and failures into corrective lessons. As new evidence accumulates, individual skill claims can be supported, contradicted, replaced, or retired. On SkillFlow benchmark, KEEL improves task success by 4.2 to 21.7 percentage points over the no-knowledge baseline, compared with gains of 2.4 to 9.6 points from SkillFlow's default method. Ablations show that skills and lessons are complementary. These results show that reliable continual agent learning depends not simply on accumulating experience, but on continually validating and evolving the knowledge derived from it. Our code is available at: https://github.com/microsoft/KEEL-TTCL26.
items.title: Holding a Steady Course: Knowledge Evolution from Expertise and Lessons for Continual Agent Learning

items.summary: SimilCode Benchmark is a curated dataset of 120 short source-code snippets in C# and Java, organised into 60 test-case pairs per language across four ground-truth similarity categories (identical, functional, structural, and different) with fifteen reference groups per language. Every pair was independently classified by two raters blind to the original labels, with near-perfect inter-rater agreement (Cohen's κ = 0.989). All code was authored specifically for this study or drawn from the public domain; no student-submitted code is included. The dataset was used to benchmark four contemporary commercial large language models as similarity analysts — claude-opus-5 , gpt-5.5-2026-04-23 , gemini-3.1-pro-preview and deepseek-v4-pro — with three independent replicates per case–model combination, yielding 1,440 evaluations. The same 120 pairs were also processed with three established classical detectors drawn from three distinct algorithmic families: Moss (winnowing fingerprints), JPlag v6.3.0 (token-string matching) and Dolos v2.9.3 (tree-sitter syntax trees). The record further includes a separate corpus for validating algorithmic-complexity (Big O) estimation: 40 canonical algorithms and 8 adversarial cases designed to defeat surface cues such as misleading identifiers, unreachable code and memoisation. Raw model responses, classical-detector outputs, the standardised prompt with its SHA-256 checksum, the ground-truth tables and the analysis scripts are published together for reproducibility.

items.summary: Replication package for the paper "Risk, not sunshine: financing costs drive the price of reliable solar-plus-storage electricity in the Middle East and North Africa" (Younas Khan and Štefan Bojnec). WHAT THIS IS Code, input data, result tables, figures and a supplementary data workbook for an hourly solar-plus-battery cost comparison of 19 Middle East and North African countries (24 sites: the 19 capitals plus five interior desert sites). The study decomposes the cross-country cost gap into cost of capital, regional equipment price and solar yield, and tests the result against finance shocks, 24 weather years, CMIP6 climate change and Monte Carlo uncertainty. The manuscript itself is not part of this deposit. CONTENTS - code/: all analysis scripts (photovoltaic model, hourly dispatch and design search, climate factors, 24-weather-year test, build-out link, decomposition, bootstrap, Monte Carlo, figures, supplementary tables) and run_all.sh, which reproduces everything in about 6 minutes on one core. - data/inputs/: the input data the scripts read (NASA POWER weather, CMIP6 point extracts, IRENA and SIPRI data, demand and footprint indicators). - results/: result tables (CSV) and results.json, which holds every number quoted in the paper. - outputs/Supplementary_Data.xlsx: a workbook with one sheet for each supplementary table (S1–S26). - outputs/figures/: the figures generated by the code (PNG and PDF). - README.md: step-by-step instructions, a map from each figure and table to its script, and the provenance and terms of each input file. HOW TO REUSE Install the packages in requirements.txt (Python 3.13), then run ./run_all.sh. All random draws use fixed seeds, so a rerun with the default 2,000 Monte Carlo draws reproduces results.json. LICENCE AND THIRD-PARTY DATA The code is released under the MIT licence and the derived results and workbook under CC BY 4.0. items.summary: Contents Folder Contents data/discovery/ Repository metadata and discovery scores for 500 projects. data/analysis/ The 1,500-record human–LLM dataset, 17,180 additional LLM classifications, classification inputs and counts for 117 repositories. data/extraction_used/ Per-repository exports of the analyzed candidates. data/manual_classify/ Master classification sheet and human–LLM comparison sheets. data/survey/ Category-level and demographic survey aggregates. protocol/ Taxonomy categories, LLM instructions, output schema and workbook prompts. scripts/archive/ Repository discovery, historical SATD extraction and LLM classification scripts. provenance/mining_logs/ Compressed SATD extraction logs. results/computed/ RQ1 and RQ2 counts, repository distributions, false-positive counts and RQ3 aggregates. figures/ AI-CPS taxonomy and practitioner criticality figures. survey/ Practitioner questionnaire. Setup Install Python and Git. Open a terminal in the folder containing requirements.txt , then install the Python dependencies: python -m pip install -r requirements.txt Repository discovery Run the discovery script to generate a repository metadata CSV: python scripts/archive/discover_repositories_original.py --output repos_for_satd.csv --max-repos 500 --include-readme The command exports up to 500 repositories and includes README inspection. Other available settings are listed with: python scripts/archive/discover_repositories_original.py --help For authenticated GitHub requests, set the GITHUB_TOKEN environment variable before running the script. Historical SATD extraction Run the miner on the supplied repository list: python scripts/archive/mine_satd_original.py --input data/discovery/repos_for_satd.csv --output-dir satd_results --repo-cache tmp_repos --log-dir satd_logs --since-year 2022 The script traverses available commits from the specified year, retrieves marker-bearing deleted source lines and their available pre-change context, and writes per-repository CSV files and logs. tmp_repos is the script's temporary clone directory. LLM classification In scripts/archive/llm_classification.py , replace the input, output and sample-count placeholders. For example, to classify the additional input: INPUT_FILE = r"data/analysis/additional_input_17180.csv" OUTPUT_FILE = r"new_additional_llm_results.csv" MAX_SAMPLES = 17180 To use the initial subset instead, set INPUT_FILE to data/analysis/manual_input_1500.csv and MAX_SAMPLES to 1500 . The sample count must be an integer. Set the OPENAI_API_KEY environment variable, then run: python scripts/archive/llm_classification.py The script reads ID , SATD_Keyword , SATD_Comment , Context_Type and Context_Code , and saves broad classifications, AI-CPS categories and proposed category names. Checkpoints are saved beside the output. To resume an interrupted run, use the same input, settings and output path. Results The supplied summaries are in results/computed/ . RQ1 percentages exclude false positives; RQ2 percentages use the AI-CPS-specific total within each analysis. Figures are supplied as PDFs in figures/ .

items.summary: TEMPLATE-DIRECTED MASS FABRICATION OF BIOMEDICAL MICRO/NANOROBOTS AT THE LIMIT is a 770-page, high-density English research monograph on scaling template replication without losing dimensional fidelity, surface integrity, functional consistency or scientific traceability. The book treats the template as a stateful manufacturing ancestor rather than a passive tool. Every cavity and replication cycle is registered so that template wear, release-coating decay, demolding force, replica bias, particle residue, spatial defect clustering and functional outcomes can be linked across the full template life. Its central falsifiable claim asks whether lifetime-aware monitoring can predict rising defect probability before damage spreads. Thirty mathematically distinct research plates cover cavity filling, squeeze flow, material relaxation, cure conversion, shrinkage, residual stress, adhesion, demolding, fracture, Archard wear, coating survival, hidden wear states, geometry transfer, Hausdorff error, spatial point processes, defect ancestry, survival hazards, change points, capability, conservative yield, hierarchical variance and qualified-part cost. Across 82 chapters and 410 single-page studies, the monograph develops replication physics, release mechanics, template wear, spatial defect genealogy, adaptive process control, functional qualification, lifecycle economics and independent transfer. Two hundred Research Gates define blind challenges, strong comparators, evidence packages, hard stops and successor forks. Thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos present genuinely different witnesses, challenge artifacts, estimators, controllers, economic falsifiers, release keys and handoff kits. The work is explicitly nonclinical and hypothesis-generating. It does not claim a completed manufacturing campaign, human treatment, autonomous in-body efficacy or regulatory approval. Its release rule is conjunctive: wear, demolding force, geometry, defect clustering, unselected yield, task function and traceability must pass together over the complete template life. items.summary: Host-based intrusion detectors order events, window audit streams and sequence attack stages by their timestamps. Every conclusion they draw therefore rests on assumptions about clocks, delivery, entity identity and the integrity of the evidence, and most of these assumptions go unstated. This Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) makes them explicit. Drawing on temporal databases, stream processing and runtime verification, we distill five components of a time model, together with a checklist of evidence assumptions and four levels of guarantee, and walk through a running campaign with them. A documented search yields fifteen families of detection and investigation. For papers selected by screening role and period, plus named systems and landmarks, we check the stated assumptions in the full texts, and we assess eleven temporal knowledge representation and reasoning (KRR) formalisms and a learned baseline on nine attack patterns. Some early alert correlators stated clock and delivery assumptions, and forensics measures clock error. Current provenance-based detectors state no clock bound. Four audited papers describe input-ordering conditions or conventions, but none specifies conditions for conclusion validity across a stated class of delivery failures. In the selected provenance-based systems, campaign composition uses system-specific procedures or objectives, learned state, causal graph queries or language models, and beyond CEP-based query systems, we found no temporal rule language or stream reasoner from KRR applied to host audit data. In 28 of 38 audited provenance-era detector papers, capture or stored evidence is trusted or its manipulation is placed out of scope, and none says which conclusions survive deleted, delayed or forged records. Five open challenges follow from these gaps.
items.title: SoK: Timestamps Are Not a Time Model: Rethinking Temporal Reasoning in Host-Based Intrusion Detection

items.summary: Continual graph learning (CGL) maintains models as graphs evolve without retraining from scratch, while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Existing methods typically target either transductive or inductive settings and often store past subgraphs or require task identifiers at inference. We propose Community-aware Prototype Extraction for Continual Graph Learning (CoPE-CGL), a replay-free framework that uses a parameter-free structural prior, precomputed by multi-hop Laplacian smoothing, to anchor learning, memory, and inference. CoPE-CGL combines topology-infused bottleneck adaptation, community-level prototypes, and dynamic routing by majority vote over node-to-prototype matches. The default protocol assumes each test graph comes from one learned task; a node-level variant handles mixed-task graphs. Each task adds at most a constant amount of storage, with no past graph data retained. At equal storage and without task identifiers, CoPE-CGL matches the strongest replay baseline even when it receives true task identifiers: average performance (AP) is 95.17% and 95.72% versus 94.28% and 95.82% on Arxiv and CoraFull, respectively, with 5.9-14.0 times faster runtime and zero forgetting. Across four transductive and three inductive benchmarks and mixed streams, CoPE-CGL exceeds the second-best of up to eleven baselines by up to 1.41, 6.32, and 9.33 AP percentage points, respectively. It runs 1.3-7.9 times faster end-to-end than the most accurate competitor on each benchmark and scales to the largest benchmark graph. On graphs mixing two tasks, its node-level variant achieves the best AP among CGL methods. The design targets homophilic graphs with community structure.
items.title: CoPE-CGL: Community-aware Prototype Extraction for Replay-Free Continual Graph Learning

items.summary: Many mathematical research agents focus on solving problems with fixed statements. However, conjecture research, especially in applied mathematics, may require revising candidate questions or conclusions as investigation proceeds, coupling problem formulation with proof development. We present PACE, a research-proof agent that supports this process through a structured research loop that selects mathematical objectives and develops or challenges candidate mechanisms. The whole prover constructs proofs from these mechanisms, and an independent verifier checks them against the original target. Evidence-tracking memory stores assumptions and dependencies arising during research and marks evidence for revalidation when a candidate or condition changes. This memory supports task-specific context composition that keeps checked premises, exploratory material and unresolved obligations distinct. To evaluate proof construction and conjecture research, we introduce ResearchProofBench, an applied-mathematics benchmark focused on optimization, comprising 51 known-proof tasks with 331 hidden checkpoints under historical abstract access and six open-problem cases. The known-proof tasks assess reconstruction of published results, while the open-problem cases assess mathematical investigation and proof development. On the 51 known-proof tasks, PACE achieves an aggregate Proof Score of 75.16 and completes 20 proofs. In conjecture research, PACE develops conditional results, with its submissions receiving higher review scores than the compared baselines.
items.title: PACE: Research Proving Agent for Adaptive Conjecture Exploration

items.summary: A staged, reproducible pipeline for VLT/MUSE narrow-field-mode integral-field data: raw-cube reduction, spectral extraction of a faint companion next to a much brighter primary star with six independent extraction schemes, and hydrogen-line accretion analysis with detection limits calibrated against empirical nulls from control positions processed identically to the object. Every stage emits a machine-readable quality-control document, and later stages read those documents rather than trusting assumptions; provenance (input cube, SHA-256 hashes, specification version, wavelength frame, flux unit) travels with the products. Research code under active development. This is the version used in Ramírez Reyes & Cáceres (in preparation).

items.summary: Web-connected sensing applications continuously generate multivariate time series with evolving behavioral categories, making Time Series Class-Incremental Learning (TSCIL) essential for adapting to new classes without forgetting previously acquired knowledge. However, preserving diverse and evolving class distributions under strict privacy and memory constraints remains a fundamental challenge. Existing approaches often face a trade-off between retaining sufficient historical knowledge for accurate recognition and minimizing the memory required for continual adaptation. To address these limitations, we propose TRACE, a memory-efficient, replay-free framework that preserves class-specific knowledge through generative modeling rather than sample rehearsal. TRACE employs a compact, frozen temporal-spectral representation and lightweight class-specific autoencoders to capture complex intra-class variations. By independently preserving each class model, TRACE avoids recursive generation and catastrophic forgetting, while enabling direct classification through reconstruction-based scoring without retaining historical samples or large statistical matrices. Extensive experiments across five TSCIL benchmarks demonstrate that TRACE achieves competitive classification accuracy while reducing mean retained memory by approximately 98.26% compared with TS-ACL, the strongest evaluated analytical baseline, and achieving an approximately 33.43% relative improvement in accuracy on GrabMyo.
items.title: TRACE: Memory-Efficient Time Series Class-Incremental Learning via Temporal-Spectral Reconstruction
